q: In plain words, a Monte Carlo simulation …
o: finds an exact answer with algebra
plays a situation out many times at random and averages the results
picks the single most likely outcome
tries every possible combination of inputs
why: Random play-throughs, then an average: that is the whole method.

q: You flip a coin 20 times and get 13 heads. What is your estimate of P(heads)? (decimal)
What is the expected value (long-run average) of one roll of a fair six-sided die?
The expected value of a die roll is a number you will often roll.
why: Myth. You can never roll 3.5; the expected value is a long-run average, not a likely single result.

q: An indicator is 1 when a project is late and 0 otherwise. Its average over 1,000 runs is 0.3. This means …
o: the estimated probability of being late is 30%
why: The average of a 0/1 variable is the share of 1s, which estimates a probability.

q: Two dice: how many of the 36 equally likely pairs give a total of 10 or more?
The law of large numbers says the average of many independent random results gets closer to the expected value.
why: True: that is why averaging many runs works.

q: How many times more runs do you need to halve the standard error?
why: The error shrinks with √N, so halving it needs √N to double: 4× the runs.

q: Single results have SD 2. What is the standard error of their average over N = 10,000 runs?
A million runs guarantee an accurate answer.
why: Myth. More runs shrink only the computing error; a wrong model or wrong inputs give a precisely computed wrong answer.
